shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per capita, PPP (current international $)
shots.narration: Since 2000, at least twenty-one countries have passed Mexico in output per person, adjusted for prices, and stayed ahead. {p} Poland in 2002. Argentina, despite all its crises, in 2005. Turkey in 2008. Then Romania, Bulgaria, Serbia. {p} China in 2023. And in 2025, Thailand and Azerbaijan. {p} Back in 2000, the average Mexican was richer than the average Pole, Turk, Thai or Chinese. {pp} Mexico isn't collapsing. It's barely moving. After inflation, the average Mexican produces only about seven percent more than in 2000. The world average grew about seventy.

And Mexico has a lot going for it. {p} A two-thousand-mile border with the biggest economy on Earth. A free-trade deal with it since 1994. Factory wages that are a fraction of American ones. More than a hundred and thirty million people. When that trade deal began, many expected Mexico to close the gap with its northern neighbors fast. {p} Today, America buys more goods from Mexico than from any other country, including China. {p} So why is everyone else pulling ahead? {pp} <soft>The answer hides in one number.</soft>

shots.src: World Bank WDI · merchandise exports (current US$, billions) · manufactures (% of merchandise exports)
shots.narration: Start with the good news, because there's a lot of it. {p} In 2000, Mexico sold about a hundred and sixty-six billion dollars of goods to the world. In 2025: about six hundred and sixty-five billion. Four times as much. Exports went from about a quarter of the economy to about forty percent. {p} More than four fifths of that is manufactured goods: cars, auto parts, televisions, computers. {pp} On this chart, Mexico's line climbs faster than Poland's or Turkey's. {p} Mexico now exports almost twice as many manufactured goods as the rest of Latin America combined.

shots.src: Congressional Research Service IF11175 (13 Aug 2026): US goods imports from Mexico $534.8 bn in 2025, first among US suppliers · World Bank WDI · FDI net inflows (% of GDP)
shots.title: US goods imports from Mexico, 2025
shots.narration: And almost all of it goes north. {p} In 2025, the United States bought about five hundred and thirty-five billion dollars of goods from Mexico, more than from China, more than from Canada. Mexico first overtook China as America's top supplier in 2023, and it has stayed there. Foreign companies keep investing about two and a half percent of Mexico's GDP every year. {pp} If you've bought a pickup truck or a flat-screen TV in America, there's a good chance it crossed that border.

stats.label: bought by the US from Mexico, 2025

shots.src: World Bank WDI · GDP per person employed (constant 2021 PPP $)
shots.narration: Now the number. Take everything Mexico produces, and divide it by the number of people who work. {p} In 2000, the average Mexican worker produced about fifty-four thousand dollars a year, adjusted for prices. That was more than a Polish worker, and more than a Turkish one. {p} By 2025, about forty-eight thousand. Down about ten percent in twenty-five years. Over the same period, workers across Latin America gained about fifteen percent. Even Brazil's gained more than a fifth. That's not a rounding error. It's twenty-five years of going nowhere. {pp} Polish and Turkish workers now produce about twice as much. And China's workers have caught up, almost to the dollar.

Think about how strange that is. {p} Exports quadrupled. Factories boomed. Foreign companies poured in. {p} And yet the average worker produces less than a generation ago. All of Mexico's growth since 2000 came from adding more workers, not from each worker producing more. Mexico's population grew by more than thirty million in that time. {p} How is that even possible? {pp} <soft>Because there isn't one Mexico. There are two.</soft>
Quick favor: if you're finding this interesting, hit subscribe. It's free, and it's genuinely what keeps this channel going. {p} Now, meet the two Mexicos.

shots.src: INEGI ENOE (Q4 2025): labor informality 55.0%; informal jobs +493,821 in 2025 (via El Economista / El Imparcial, 25 Feb 2026) · OECD Revenue Statistics 2025 (Mexico: lowest tax-to-GDP ratio in the OECD)
shots.title: Mexico's workers, end of 2025
shots.narration: The first Mexico is the one in the export numbers: big, modern factories, mostly in the north and center, as productive as many in the United States. {p} The second Mexico is everyone else. {p} More than half of Mexico's workers are informal: street vendors, family shops, day laborers. No contract, no social security, and almost no machines. Many stay small on purpose, because growing means paying taxes and social security contributions. {pp} In 2025, informal jobs grew by almost half a million. The modern Mexico is world-class. It just doesn't employ most Mexicans. {p} It also means Mexico collects less tax, relative to its economy, than any other country in the OECD club of rich and middle-income democracies.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · intentional homicides (per 100,000 people)
shots.narration: Then there's violence. {p} In 2007, Mexico had about eight murders per hundred thousand people. {p} After the government declared war on the drug cartels, that rate more than tripled, to about twenty-nine by 2018. It has eased since, to about twenty-five in 2023. That's still three times the 2007 level. {pp} Every business pays for that, in guards, in bribes, in stolen trucks, and in investments that never happen.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · poverty headcount at national poverty lines (INEGI/CONEVAL multidimensional measure) · CONASAMI: general minimum wage 88.36 pesos/day (2018) → 278.80 (2025) · personal remittances received (BX.TRF.PWKR)
shots.narration: But here's the twist. Mexicans got less poor anyway. {p} In 2018, about forty-two percent of Mexicans lived in poverty, by the official measure. By 2024, about thirty percent. That's more than thirteen million fewer people in poverty. {p} The biggest reason: wages at the bottom. Mexico's minimum wage went from about eighty-eight pesos a day in 2018 to almost two hundred and eighty in 2025. More than triple. {pp} Prices rose too, but nowhere near that much. A universal pension for everyone over sixty-five helped too. And Mexicans working in the United States sent home about sixty-five billion dollars in 2025, about three and a half percent of the economy.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · Gini index (0 = perfect equality) · unemployment (modeled ILO estimate)
shots.narration: Inequality fell too. {p} Mexico's Gini index, a standard measure of how unequal incomes are, dropped from about fifty-three in 2000 to under forty-three in 2024. Brazil's is still about fifty. That's a remarkable change in a single generation. {p} And unemployment is under three percent, lower than in the United States. Almost everyone who wants a job has one. {pp} The problem was never that Mexicans don't work. It's that too many of them work in jobs that produce very little.

shots.src: World Bank WDI · gross fixed capital formation (% of GDP) · female labor force participation (% of women 15+) · OECD PISA 2022
shots.narration: So what would it take? {p} First, investment. Mexico invests about a fifth of its economy each year, barely more than in 2000. Turkey, almost a third. China, about two fifths. {p} Second, women. Fewer than half of Mexican women are in the labor force, below the rich-country average. Third, schools: Mexican teenagers score near the bottom of the OECD's PISA tests. {p} And fourth, moving workers from the second Mexico into the first, which means credit, roads, schools, and above all, safety.

The opportunity is enormous. As companies move factories out of China, Mexico is the closest alternative to the American market. {p} It already has the factories, the trade deal, and the workers. {p} What it hasn't had, for twenty-five years, is growth that reaches the average worker. In 2025, the whole economy grew just half a percent. {p} It doesn't need a miracle. Poland raised output per worker almost three percent a year, for twenty-five years. {pp} <soft>Twenty-one countries have shown it can be done. Mexico has the map.</soft> {p} It just has to use it.
One of those twenty-one countries did it with fifty percent inflation. To see how, watch this next. {p} I'm Chartbound. See you in the next one.

yt.title: Mexico Exports 4x More Than in 2000. Its Workers Produce Less.
yt.description:
Since 2000, at least 21 countries have passed Mexico in GDP per person adjusted for prices and stayed ahead, from Poland and Turkey to China and Thailand. Mexico's exports quadrupled and it became America's #1 supplier, yet output per worker fell about 10% in 25 years. Why: two Mexicos (world-class factories vs. an informal majority), violence, and low investment. The twist: poverty and inequality fell sharply anyway.

Sources: World Bank WDI (NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.CD, NY.GDP.PCAP.PP.KD, TX.VAL.MRCH.CD.WT, TX.VAL.MANF.ZS.UN, SL.GDP.PCAP.EM.KD, VC.IHR.PSRC.P5, SI.POV.NAHC, SI.POV.GINI, SL.UEM.TOTL.ZS, NE.GDI.FTOT.ZS, SL.TLF.CACT.FE.ZS, FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG); INEGI ENOE; Congressional Research Service (US–Mexico trade); CONASAMI (minimum wage).
